narration: A distinction from philosophy helps here. In 1995, the philosopher Ned Block separated access consciousness from phenomenal consciousness. Access is information available for reasoning, for report and for action. Phenomenal consciousness is experience: what it is like. Some philosophers dispute the distinction, and whether either can come without the other is debated.
visual_description: Two circles of light on a dark ground, one in the upper left and one in the lower right: the upper one a solid disc with a clean edge, the lower one a round glow that fades out softly with no edge. Between them lies a faint overlap in which the two halos fade into each other, so that it is not clear where one ends and the other begins. Muted teal and warm amber, wide negative space. No text.

concept: What the study does not show
narration: The researchers are careful about where their study stops. They write that their experiments do not show that Claude can have experiences, or feel things in the way humans do. They add that it is unclear whether any scientific experiment could prove this to be true or false. They think the findings say something about access, not experience.
visual_description: A single calm line of pale gold light running across a dark ground and ending at a soft boundary, beyond which there is only a smooth, dim, empty area with no shapes in it; the line neither crosses nor turns back. Deep indigo, pale gold, very low contrast, wide empty space. No text.

narration: They describe the J-lens as an imperfect method. It captures only concepts that match single word pieces, and the researchers do not know what decides which concepts enter the J-space. What the lens shows is only part of the picture.
visual_description: A magnifying glass with no handle, lying tilted on a dark table. Through it, a small circle of the table's own plain grain shows larger; everywhere else the table is smooth and empty. Nothing is printed anywhere. Warm grey, soft amber, quiet shadows. No people, no text.

narration: The researchers set out how the model's workspace differs from the brain's, as the theory describes it. There, the workspace is sustained by loops of signals cycling back over time. The model's works in a single pass through its layers, so that depth, the step from layer to layer, stands in for time.
visual_description: A split frame on a dark background. Left: a small ring of dots with a pulse that travels round the ring again and again, caption 'time'. Right: a straight vertical stack of layers with a single pulse rising once from bottom to top, caption 'depth'. Only two words on screen, slow motion.

narration: There are two more differences. Human working memory, the mind's short-term holding space, fades within seconds, while the model can look back at anything earlier in the text. And human conscious contents come as images, sounds and planned movements, whereas the model's workspace is built almost entirely of words.
visual_description: One frame divided by a thin vertical line: on the left, ripples spreading and fading on dark still water; on the right, a long ribbon of pale strokes (not letters) stretching away into the distance, each stroke equally clear. Blue-black water, silver ripples, cream ribbon, wide dark margins. No text.

narration: Researchers also differ on what consciousness depends on. Global workspace theory is a functional theory: it is about what a system does, not what it is made of. Others think consciousness may depend on more than function, for example on living biology, or on the physical structure of a system. Which view is right is not known.
visual_description: A fork in a path through a quiet forest at dusk: one branch runs between living trees and moss, the other across smooth, geometric stone slabs; both lead gently into a pale, empty distance. Deep green and slate, soft grey where the paths end, plenty of empty space. No people, no text.

narration: Outside experts were invited to comment on the study. Commentaries came from Stanislas Dehaene and Lionel Naccache; from Patrick Butlin, Dillon Plunkett, Robert Long and Derek Shiller; and from Neel Nanda, whose commentary includes an independent replication of some findings on an open-weight model, one outsiders can study from the inside. Their commentaries are best read in their own words.
visual_description: A long oval table seen from above in warm lamplight, with six or seven empty chairs around it and loose sheets of paper scattered on its surface. No people. Dark wood, cream paper, amber light, soft shadows. No text.
